lead: Real gases deviate from PV = nRT because molecules occupy space and attract one another. The virial equation writes the deviation as a series in 1/V or in P. Cubic equations such as van der Waals add two physical corrections: a finite molecular volume b and an attraction term a/V². Engineers use them to size gas lines and storage vessels when the ideal gas law is too rough.
prereq: You need: the ideal gas law and the critical constants Tc and Pc from the phase diagram.

sections.h3: Compressibility factor and the virial series

blocks.text: Z = PV/RT is 1 for an ideal gas at every pressure. For a real gas it departs from 1 because molecules attract and occupy volume. The virial equation is an exact infinite series for that departure:

blocks.where: Z is PV/(RT); V is molar volume in L/mol; P is pressure in bar; B is the second virial coefficient in L/mol; C is the third virial coefficient in L²/mol²; B' and C' are pressure-series coefficients with units 1/bar and 1/bar².

blocks.text: B comes from pair interactions, C from three-body interactions. B depends strongly on temperature: negative at low temperature, where attraction dominates, and positive at high temperature. The two series are linked by B′ = B/RT and C′ = (C − B²)/(RT)². At moderate pressure the series can be cut after B: Z ≈ 1 + B/V or Z ≈ 1 + BP/RT. This truncated virial equation serves gas metering and moderate-pressure densities, not dense liquids. Some syllabi call this the mathematical representation of PVT behaviour.
The van der Waals equation replaces the ideal-gas pressure RT/V with two terms:

blocks.where: P is pressure in bar; V is molar volume in L/mol; T is temperature in K; R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ when V is in m³/mol and P is in Pa, or R = 0.08314 L bar mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ when V is in L/mol and P is in bar; b is the excluded volume per mole in L/mol; a is the attraction parameter in L² bar mol⁻².

blocks.text: RT/(V − b) is the pressure of hard molecules of finite size; b is the excluded volume per mole, about four times the molecules' own volume. The term −a/V² lowers the pressure because attraction pulls molecules back from the wall. As V grows, both corrections fade and the equation tends to PV = RT.

At the critical point the T = T<sub>c</sub> isotherm has a horizontal inflection. So at that one point, V = V<sub>c</sub> and P = P<sub>c</sub>, both (∂P/∂V)<sub>T</sub> = 0 and (∂²P/∂V²)<sub>T</sub> = 0. Solving these two conditions with the equation itself gives the constants:

blocks.where: T<sub>c</sub> is critical temperature in K; P<sub>c</sub> is critical pressure in bar; V<sub>c</sub> is critical molar volume in L/mol; Z<sub>c</sub> is critical compressibility factor.

blocks.text: Real fluids have Z<sub>c</sub> of 0.23 to 0.29, so van der Waals overpredicts Z<sub>c</sub> and is poor near the critical point and for dense liquids.

Put P = P<sub>r</sub>P<sub>c</sub>, V = V<sub>r</sub>V<sub>c</sub> and T = T<sub>r</sub>T<sub>c</sub> into the van der Waals equation. The constants a and b cancel. The result is the reduced van der Waals equation:

blocks.where: P<sub>r</sub> = P/P<sub>c</sub>, V<sub>r</sub> = V/V<sub>c</sub> and T<sub>r</sub> = T/T<sub>c</sub> are reduced pressure, volume and temperature; all are dimensionless.

blocks.text: This equation contains no gas-specific constant. Two fluids at the same reduced temperature and reduced pressure then have the same reduced volume, and hence the same Z: the law of corresponding states. It is the first generalized equation of state. Real fluids follow it only approximately; generalized correlations correct it.

The van der Waals equation is the simplest cubic. Redlich–Kwong (RK) divides the attraction term by T<sup>0.5</sup>: a/(T<sup>0.5</sup>V(V + b)). Soave (SRK) and Peng–Robinson (PR) make a depend on T and ω, and are the simulator defaults for gases and vapour–liquid equilibrium; mixtures need mixing rules for a and b.

sections.h3: The generic cubic and solving for volume

blocks.text: All four equations fit one pattern, which is how textbooks and simulators store them:
P = RT/(V − b) − a(T)/[(V + εb)(V + σb)],   a(T) = Ψ α(T<sub>r</sub>) R²T<sub>c</sub>²/P<sub>c</sub>,   b = Ω RT<sub>c</sub>/P<sub>c</sub>
blocks.where: ε, σ, Ω and Ψ are pure numbers fixed for each equation; α(T<sub>r</sub>) is a function of reduced temperature (and of ω for SRK and PR).

blocks.text: Given T and V, the pressure comes straight out. Given T and P, V is a root of a cubic; for van der Waals, PV³ − (Pb + RT)V² + aV − ab = 0. Above T<sub>c</sub> there is one real root. Below T<sub>c</sub> and inside the dome there are three: the smallest is liquid-like, the largest vapour-like, and the middle one has no physical meaning. Start Newton's method from the ideal-gas volume for the vapour root, or from V = b for the liquid root.

figure.caption: CO₂ at 300 K. At V = 1 L/mol (worked example 1) the ideal-gas law gives 24.94 bar and van der Waals 22.41 bar. At 40 bar (worked example 2) the ideal gas needs 0.6236 L/mol but the van der Waals root is 0.4996 L/mol, so Z = 0.801.

spec.aria: Pressure from 0 to 90 bar against molar volume from 0.3 to 2 litres per mole for carbon dioxide at 300 kelvin. The solid ideal-gas curve lies above the dashed van der Waals curve. At 1 litre per mole the points are 24.94 and 22.41 bar. A dashed line at 40 bar meets the van der Waals curve at 0.4996 and the ideal curve at 0.6236 litres per mole.

examples.question: For CO<sub>2</sub> at 300 K and V = 1.00 L/mol, use R = 0.08314 L·bar/(mol·K), a = 3.640 L²·bar/mol² and b = 0.04267 L/mol. Find P from the ideal gas law and from the van der Waals equation.
steps: van der Waals: first compute V − b = 1.00 − 0.04267 = 0.95733 L/mol.
Subtract: P = 26.054 − 3.640 = 22.414 bar, which rounds to 22.41 bar.
examples.answer: The ideal gas law gives 24.94 bar and the van der Waals equation gives 22.41 bar.
examples.check:
R = 0.08314
T = 300.0
V = 1.00
a = 3.640
b = 0.04267
P<sub>ideal</sub> = R * T / V
P<sub>vdw</sub> = R * T / (V - b) - a / V**2
print(round(P<sub>ideal,</sub> 2))
print(round(P<sub>vdw,</sub> 2))

examples.question: The same CO<sub>2</sub> is held at 300 K and 40.0 bar. Find its molar volume and Z from the van der Waals equation (same a and b), and compare with the ideal gas.
steps: Ideal gas first, as the starting guess: V<sub>0</sub> = RT/P = 0.08314 × 300/40.0 = 0.6236 L/mol.
Write the cubic: f(V) = PV³ − (Pb + RT)V² + aV − ab, with Pb + RT = 40.0 × 0.04267 + 24.942 = 26.649 and ab = 3.640 × 0.04267 = 0.15532. Its slope is f′(V) = 3PV² − 2(Pb + RT)V + a.

Repeat until the change is below 10<sup>−5</sup> L/mol (table below): the root is V = 0.4996 L/mol. 300 K is just below the van der Waals T<sub>c</sub> of 304 K, but 40 bar is far below its saturation pressure, so this is the only vapour root.
examples.answer: V = 0.4996 L/mol and Z = 0.801: the gas takes about 20 % less room than the ideal-gas 0.6236 L/mol.

traps: Putting V instead of (V − b) in the repulsion term; b must be subtracted from molar volume before dividing.
Mixing units: R = 0.08314 needs V in L/mol and P in bar, while R = 8.314 needs V in m³/mol and P in Pa. Convert before substituting.
Using a and b of one gas with P, V, T data of another gas. a and b are gas-specific.
Forcing van der Waals near the critical point or for a dense liquid; it is poor there. Use a better cubic or generalized correlation.

quiz.q: In Z = PV/(RT), what does Z equal for an ideal gas, and what is the second virial coefficient B?
quiz.a: For an ideal gas Z = 1. B is the coefficient of the 1/V term; it accounts for pair interactions and has units of volume per mole, such as L/mol.

quiz.q: Why does the term −a/V² lower the pressure in the van der Waals equation?
quiz.a: Attraction between molecules pulls them toward the bulk and reduces the force they exert on the wall. The measured pressure is lower than the hard-sphere pressure RT/(V − b).

quiz.q: Why can a cubic equation give three volume roots at one T and P below T<sub>c</sub>, and which roots are physical?
quiz.a: Below T<sub>c</sub> the isotherm has a loop. The smallest root is the liquid and the largest the vapour; the middle root lies where (∂P/∂V)<sub>T</sub> > 0, which is unstable and has no meaning.

quiz.q: For CO2 at 300 K and V = 2.00 L/mol, use R = 0.08314 L bar mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, a = 3.640 L² bar mol⁻², b = 0.04267 L mol⁻¹. Find P from van der Waals.

At low pressure van der Waals gives Z ≈ 1 + (b − a/RT)P/RT. For CO<sub>2</sub> (a = 3.640 L²·bar/mol², b = 0.04267 L/mol) find the temperature at which Z stays at 1 at low pressure, and the sign of Z − 1 at 300 K.
quiz.a: Z = 1 when b = a/RT, the Boyle temperature T<sub>B</sub> = a/(Rb) = 3.640/(0.08314 × 0.04267) = 1026 K. At 300 K, b − a/RT = 0.04267 − 3.640/24.942 = −0.1033 L/mol, so Z < 1: attraction wins.

beyond: Not for the exam. Process simulators use Peng–Robinson and SRK as default property packages for hydrocarbons, and add association terms for water, alcohols and CO<sub>2</sub>-rich mixtures. Search next for cubic equation of state mixing rules and the second virial coefficient.
